sources.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. 2017. A phonological comparison of Gamale, Sheram and Ghusbang - three Kham varieties. JSEALS 10(1): 67-90. hdl 10524/52398
sources.note: Suprasegmentals sections (§2.2.3 Sheram p.75, §2.3.3 Ghusbang, §3.3 p.83) treat only modal/breathy phonation and non-contrastive length and pitch; stress never mentioned. Author codes the varieties kgj/kjl; Sheram is not Sheshi (Watters' classification puts Sheshi = Jangkot/Tapnang).

sources.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. 2016. Gamale Kham phonology revisited, with Devanagari-based orthography and lexicon. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 9: 130-199. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics, ANU. hdl 1885/109195. ISSN 1836-6821.
sources.note: Nothing about Sheshi. For Gamale (gama1251) sec. 2.3 'Suprasegmentals' (p. 137 of the journal = PDF the text layerff.) states: 'Gamale Kham contrasts between modal (14a) and breathy (14b) phonation.. Unlike Takale Kham as described by Watters (1971; 1985; 2002), Gamale Kham is an atonal language. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (15a-b) [kuŋ32 yoke vs kuŋ53 hole]'; sec. 3.3 repeats this for the orthography (high pitch left unmarked as 'extremely rare'). The word 'stress' does not occur in the article. Tense phonation posited in Wilde 2011 is withd…

sources.citation: Namkung, Ju (ed.). 1996. Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages. (STEDT Monograph Series 3.) Berkeley: Sino-Tibetan Etymological Dictionary and Thesaurus Project, University of California. xxviii+507 pp. [Kham entries pp. 175-177]
sources.note: Four-way TONES table ('ma tense pitch pattern 1 clear voice; 'mah lax pitch pattern 1 breathy; ma tense pitch pattern 2 clear; mah lax pitch pattern 2 creaky) and a note that Kham tone is a word-level correlate of pitch pattern and register: pattern 1 = high level on the stem + low on the suffix, pattern 2 = falling on the stem + mid on the suffix; refers to Hale 1973 pp. 20-22 for detail. Nothing on stress. Applies to Takale Kham only.

sources.citation: Watters, Stephen. 2018. Linguistic identity and dialect diversity: a conundrum with regard to Magar Kham. In Language and Identity in a Multilingual, Migrating World. Dallas: SIL International
sources.note: Sociolinguistic intelligibility study covering Sheshi [kip]; may point to unpublished Sheshi phonological data (S. Watters 1988 profile).

sources.citation: Pokhrel, Lalmani (पोख्रेल, लालमणि). 2014. मगर पाङ (भाषा) को अध्ययन १ [A study of the Magar Pang (Kham) language, part 1]. Samakalin Sahitya (समकालीन साहित्य प्रतिष्ठान, UK), online, 20 September 2014; web serialisation of a Nepali-language monograph based on fieldwork in Rolpa, Poush-Magh 2063 BS (2006-07); part 2 announced.
sources.note: No statement on tone (तान/सुर) or stress (बलाघात/आघात) anywhere in part 1. Content: history/naming of Magar Pang, dialect areas, speaker numbers, institutional efforts, long verb lists with Nepali glosses, local social-dialect vocabulary. The reproduced monograph TOC lists §3.6 with examples of meaning differences by 'दीर्घ, अतिदीर्घ (ः), महाप्राणत्व ( ं) तथा व्यतिरेकी उच्चारण' (length, over-length, aspiration, contrastive pronunciation; p. 86 of the print work), but that section's text is not in the posted part.

sources.citation: Sapkota, Suren. 2013. A sociolinguistic survey of Magar-Kham. Kathmandu: Linguistic Survey of Nepal (LinSuN), Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University. 143 pp.
sources.note: Glottolog's reference for shes1236; a LinSuN survey with wordlists across Kham varieties; unlikely to state stress but the only recent Sheshi-area fieldwork.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul (ed.). 2009. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 16th edition, entry 'Kham, Sheshi' [kip]; and Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds.) 2015, 18th edition, entry 'Kham, Sheshi' [kip]. Dallas: SIL International. (the Internet Archive copies of the web entries.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No typology line and nothing on tone or stress in either the 16th- or 18th-edition kip entry: population 20,000 (2003), village list, dialects Tapnanggi/Jangkoti, '30% intelligibility levels with Gamale Kham [kgj], and even less with Western Parbate [kjl]', lexical similarity 55/51/46%, literacy, Devanagari script; SIL bibliography item cited: Watters 2005.

sources.citation: Acharya, Bhola Nath. 2007. Sociolinguistic Study of Magar Kham Language. M.A. thesis, Central Department of English, Tribhuvan University, Kirtipur. 72 pp. TUCL eLibrary hdl 20.500.14540/7059.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology section and no statement on word stress or lexical tone. Lexical similarity: Seshi-Parbate 60%, Seshi-Gamal 70%, Seshi-Nishel 65%. The only prosodic remark is about question intonation in the generic grammar appendix (p. 51-52): 'Type I interrogative sentence is marked by only the question after the sentence.. When there is short tone after the verb then it refers to the simple sentence. When the speaker pronounce a long rising tone with the ending of the verb then it marks the interrogative' - sentence-level intonation, not word stress or lexical tone, and not attributed to Sesh…

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1997. Tibeto-Burman languages and classification. In David Bradley (ed.), Tibeto-Burman Languages of the Himalayas (Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics 14; Pacific Linguistics A-86), 1-72. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: speaker numbers and 'Extensive descriptive work has been carried out by Watters'; nothing on tone or stress

sources.citation: Rempt, Boudewijn. 1994. The verbal agreement system of four Khām languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 17(1): 1-59. DOI 10.32655/ltba.17.1.01
sources.note: Nothing on stress for any variety. §3.2 (p.11): 'Takale Kham is the only Kham language for which a phonological description exists'; §5 (p.31): 'Sheshi Kham is only known through the description provided by Watters (1991:13-15). No other studies of Sheshi Kham exist.' Sheshi section (pp.31-38) is pronouns and verb paradigms only.

sources.citation: Watters, David E. 1993. Agreement systems and syntactic organization in the Kham verb [Nepal]. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(2): 89-112. DOI 10.32655/ltba.16.2.04
sources.note: Nothing. §2 names Takale, Gamale and Sheshi as the three major dialect groupings; §3.3.3 (pp.101-103) gives Sheshi subject-agreement paradigms from a single informant (fn.7); no phonology.

sources.citation: Watters, David E. 1985. Emergent word tone in Kham: a Tibeto-Burman halfway house. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 8(2): 36-54. DOI 10.32655/ltba.8.2.02
sources.note: Takale (Taka) Kham word-tone genesis; only general remarks on unstressed/schwa prefix syllables and 'destressing' of prefixes; no stress-placement rule and nothing on Sheshi.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid shes1236; en.wikipedia 'Magar Kham language' (wikitext)
sources.note: Glottolog lists only Sapkota 2013 and Watters 2002 (dialect chapter) for shes1236; Wikipedia gives Watters' classification (Sheshi [kip]: Jangkoti, Tapnangi Kham) and no stress information.
